Apply the four checks and record each answer: the issuer's ability to pay and the state guaranty limit, the surrender period with a 7% charge meaning $14,000 on $200,000, the inflation exposure of a fixed payment with $18,000 worth $10,984.88 in today's terms after twenty years at 2.5%, and whether the account is already tax-advantaged.

lessons.title: Beneficiaries, probate, and why documents beat intentions
lessons.explanation: Money leaves an estate through one of four channels, and only one of them is the will. Contract designations transfer retirement accounts, life insurance, and payable-on-death or transfer-on-death bank accounts directly to the named beneficiary. Joint ownership with right of survivorship transfers by operation of law in many jurisdictions. A trust transfers according to its terms. Anything left over passes under the will, or under the state's intestacy statute if there is no will, and usually goes through probate, which is a court process with filings, timelines, and fees that vary by state. The consequence is that a beneficiary designation generally controls even when it contradicts the will, which is why an outdated designation is one of the most common and least visible planning failures. Two documents can disagree, and the older instruction is often the one that takes effect. On top of that sits a tax system that treats inheriting differently depending on the asset: a tax-deferred retirement account is generally income to the beneficiary when distributed, which is why the required distribution rules for inherited accounts matter so much, while other assets are treated differently again. Probate procedure, spousal rights, and state estate or inheritance taxes are matters of state law.
lessons.example: Two computations show where the paperwork turns into money. First, beneficiary designations determine how much protection a bank account gets: for trust accounts under the federal deposit insurance rules, coverage is the number of owners times the number of distinct beneficiaries times $250,000, so one owner naming three distinct beneficiaries is covered up to $750,000, while an owner naming six or more beneficiaries is capped at $1,250,000 per owner at one bank, a change effective April 1, 2024. A designation that names five people instead of three therefore changes coverage, and a designation that names the estate rather than individuals may produce a different result again. Second, inherited retirement account arithmetic: a $400,000 tax-deferred account inherited by a designated beneficiary who is not an eligible designated beneficiary is generally subject to the ten-year rule, meaning the account must be emptied within ten years of the year of death. If the beneficiary's tax rate averaged a hypothetical 24%, the income tax would be about $96,000; at a hypothetical 32% it would be about $128,000, and at 12% about $48,000. The flat-rate framing is a simplification, because real withdrawals fill brackets year by year, and the rules for eligible designated beneficiaries, spouses, and non-individual beneficiaries differ.
lessons.question: Why can a beneficiary designation override a will that says something different?
lessons.answer: Because the designation is a contract term that transfers the asset directly, outside the estate
lessons.distractor: Because the most recently signed document always controls, so the designation wins if it is newer
lessons.correction: Recency is not the mechanism. A designation on a contract moves that asset by contract, so the asset never enters the estate for the will to dispose of, regardless of which document was signed later. The will governs what remains.

depth.definitions: A beneficiary designation is the instruction on an account or policy naming who receives it. A payable-on-death or transfer-on-death designation is a similar instruction on a bank or brokerage account. Probate is the court-supervised process for administering an estate. Intestacy is the statutory distribution scheme that applies without a valid will. A personal representative, also called an executor or administrator, is the person responsible for the estate. An eligible designated beneficiary is a category in the federal required distribution rules that includes a spouse, a minor child of the account owner, a disabled or chronically ill individual, and a person not more than ten years younger than the owner. The ten-year rule requires many non-spouse beneficiaries to empty an inherited account within ten years of the year of death.
depth.mechanism: The reason designations dominate is structural: a retirement account or an insurance policy has a contract, and the contract says who gets paid. The estate only receives what the designations and ownership titles do not already remove. This creates a trap when life changes without paperwork changing, because a former spouse, a deceased parent, or a beneficiary who is now a minor can remain on a form that no one has looked at in a decade. The tax layer adds a second mechanism: because distributions from an inherited tax-deferred account are generally ordinary income to the beneficiary, the timing of the withdrawals is a planning decision with a statutory frame, and the frame differs by beneficiary category. The insurance layer adds a third: the NAIC's consumer guide advises against naming a minor child as a life insurance beneficiary because insurers will not pay a minor, and suggests directing the money to a trust or the estate instead, which changes who controls the money and when. Review the actual forms rather than the intent, because the four channels have different rules in each state and the rules change.
depth.secondExample: Two savers intend the same outcome and produce different results. The first holds a brokerage account titled in their own name with no designation and a will naming one child; the account goes through probate as part of the estate, and the will directs the distribution. The second holds the same account with a transfer-on-death designation naming the same child; the account transfers outside the estate, and the will has nothing to say about it. The economic totals may be identical and the process is not: probate is a public court proceeding with its own schedule and its own costs set by state law and by the estate's circumstances, which this course will not estimate because it varies by jurisdiction and by case. A third saver completes the transfer-on-death form and then changes the designation after a divorce, which is the scenario that produces litigation. The lesson generalizes: the transfer channel is chosen by the form, the outcome is decided by the form as it reads on the day of death, and intentions recorded anywhere else are advisory.
depth.mistake: The dominant misconception is that a will disposes of everything, which is false for every asset that carries its own designation, and a closely related error is assuming a designation made years ago still reflects a decision that was actually made. A third mistake is naming a minor as a beneficiary of a life insurance policy or retirement account without providing a mechanism for the money to be managed, which the NAIC guide addresses directly by noting that insurers will not pay a minor. A fourth is assuming the estate pays the income tax on an inherited retirement account; the beneficiary generally pays tax on distributions. The diagnostic is a one-hour exercise that costs nothing: list every account and policy, read the current designation for each, list the owner and the title, and compare the list with the will. Any item whose designation is blank, stale, or inconsistent with the will is the finding, and the list itself is the artifact.
depth.application: Build a beneficiary inventory with five columns: the asset, who owns it and how it is titled, the current designation or the absence of one, the expected tax character in the beneficiary's hands, and the transfer channel (designation, survivorship, trust, or probate). Then write one paragraph naming the three items most likely to produce an unintended result, and state what verification each requires, such as a current form from the institution or guidance from a qualified professional in the relevant jurisdiction. Model response and self-review rubric: every listed asset has a stated title and designation rather than an assumption; the tax-character column distinguishes tax-deferred accounts from the rest; at least one item is flagged as unverified and says what would verify it; the write-up states explicitly that probate, spousal rights, and estate tax rules are jurisdiction-dependent and change; and no specific tax figure is asserted without the rate assumption beside it.
depth.summary: Estate planning at this level is not about documents that sound solemn; it is about which channel each asset uses and whether the form on file still matches the intention. Designations beat intentions, inherited tax-deferred accounts carry an income tax consequence with a statutory deadline, and the procedural rules are state law. The final lesson closes the level by returning to claims made in the present tense, where all of the level's instruments and arithmetic are applied at once.

lessons.title: Capstone: audit a financial claim with the whole toolkit
lessons.explanation: The level has supplied instruments, and this lesson is the procedure that uses them together on a claim somebody is making to you. The audit has eight moves. Write the claim as numbers with units and dates, because a claim that cannot be written as numbers cannot be checked. Name the assumption behind every rate, including the horizon, the compounding convention, and whether the figure is nominal. Recompute with a tool rather than by impression, and record the result. Identify the fee, tax, and inflation treatment, or record that it is unstated. Verify the person and the product: registration status and disciplinary history for a person through the SEC's investment adviser search and FINRA's BrokerCheck, and filed disclosure documents for a fund or company through the SEC's EDGAR system. Test any guarantee against its mechanism: a guarantee has to come from somewhere with the capacity to pay, whether that is an insurer subject to state guaranty limits, a statutory deposit insurance scheme, or nobody. Record the arithmetic and the unresolved unknowns separately. Then state a bounded conclusion, which may be that the claim is arithmetically consistent but rests on an unstated assumption, or that it is not verifiable at all. The audit standard is deliberately modest: unverified is not the same as false, and the honest output names which one you have.
lessons.example: Audit this claim: a guaranteed 8% a year, so $50,000 will double in nine years. First, the arithmetic. The doubling check passes: $50,000 at 8% for nine years is $99,950.23, which is 1.999 times the starting amount, and the rule of 72 gives 72 divided by 8 equals 9 years against an exact ln 2 divided by ln 1.08 of 9.006 years. So the numbers are internally consistent. The audit defect is the guarantee and its context. A fixed 8% for twenty years would turn $10,000 into $46,609.57, while an assumed 4% turns it into $21,911.23; no deposit account or government guarantee pays that as a fixed promise, so the question becomes who is standing behind the word guaranteed. Second, the fee test: if 2.25 percentage points of costs sit inside the product, the net rate is 5.75% and $50,000 becomes $82,697.69 in nine years rather than $99,950.23, a difference of $17,252.54, and the doubling claim fails. Third, the average-return test: five hypothetical annual returns of plus 30%, minus 15%, plus 25%, minus 2% and plus 22% average 12% arithmetically and turn $50,000 into $82,571.12, a compound rate of 10.55%. A claim of a 12% return that quotes the average has overstated the compounding rate by 1.45 points without stating a false number.
lessons.question: A claim quotes an average annual return. What must you compute before accepting it as a description of growth?
lessons.answer: The compound rate produced by the same returns in sequence
lessons.distractor: The standard deviation of the returns, since volatility is what the average conceals
lessons.correction: Volatility is why the average overstates growth, but the number that answers the question is the geometric rate that actually compounds. In the example, returns averaging 12% compounded at 10.55%, and that is the figure a projection must use.

depth.definitions: An audit here means a documented recomputation and verification, not an assurance engagement. The arithmetic mean is the simple average of a series; the geometric mean is the constant rate that reproduces the multi-period outcome. Nominal figures are in current dollars; real figures are adjusted for purchasing power. A guarantee is a promise with a promisor; identifying the promisor is part of the audit. A registration check establishes that a person or firm is registered and discloses disciplinary history, not that a proposal is sound. EDGAR is the SEC's filing system, with full text search across filings. An unresolved unknown is a specific fact the audit could not determine, recorded as such.
depth.mechanism: Each instrument in the level covers a specific failure mode, and the audit is the discipline of applying them in order. The fee arithmetic catches costs that are described in percentages and priced in dollars. The nominal and real distinction catches projections that quietly ignore purchasing power. The risk and dispersion material catches the substitution of an average for a distribution. The standard-of-conduct material identifies which obligations attach and which disclosures are owed. The behavioral material identifies where the claim is designed to land, usually on recency or on the reluctance to sell at a loss. The tax and account material catches treatments that are omitted, and the insurance and annuity material catches guarantees whose promisor is unidentified. The verification step is separate from the arithmetic on purpose: a claim can be arithmetically correct and unverifiable, or arithmetically wrong and made by a registered firm. Both facts belong in the record, in their own sections.
depth.secondExample: Apply the audit to a softer claim: a document stating that a portfolio returned 9% a year over a decade, without stating whether the figure is net of fees, what the benchmark was, or whether it is time-weighted or dollar-weighted. Recompute what can be recomputed: if 9% is gross and the client paid 1.2% a year, the client's rate is approximately 7.8% before tax on a simple subtraction and about 7.71% on the exact multiplicative calculation, which changes a decade's ending value substantially; if the money was added year by year, the experience of the dollars actually invested differs from the stated rate because contributions made after strong years bought in at higher prices. The audit output here is not a verdict on the document but a list of four questions: net or gross, which benchmark, which method, and over what exact period. Two of the four are usually answerable from the document's own notes, and the audit's value is that the other two are now identified rather than assumed.
depth.mistake: The failure mode in auditing is going too far in one of two directions. The first is treating a claim as proven because the arithmetic checks out, which mistakes internal consistency for truth; the doubling arithmetic in the example is correct and the guarantee is still unsupported. The second is declaring fraud from a single discrepancy, when the honest finding is usually that a claim is unverifiable or that a material assumption is unstated. A third and subtler error is auditing the return and ignoring the promisor, which is how guarantees from unidentified sources pass review. The diagnostic is to ask, for every number in the claim, which of the three labels it currently carries: computed by you, stated by the document with an assumption, or unverified. Any number carrying the third label cannot appear in a conclusion as though it carried the first.
depth.application: Carry out one complete audit on a claim you have actually been given, whether in an advertisement, a message, or a conversation, and produce a one-page record with the eight moves labeled: the claim transcribed as numbers, the assumptions named, your recomputation with the tool and the result, the fee and tax and inflation treatment or the notation that it is unstated, the verification attempts and their outcomes for the person and the product, the guarantee and its promisor, the list of unresolved unknowns, and a bounded conclusion. Model response and self-review rubric: the transcription converts every figure into a number with a unit and a date; at least one figure is recomputed and the recomputation is shown; at least one verification attempt is documented with the source consulted, whether or not it resolved anything; the guarantee line names a promisor or states that none was identified; the unknowns are listed as questions rather than as accusations; and the conclusion uses one of the three labels for each figure, with unverified kept distinct from false. A record that concludes with a recommendation for the reader's personal situation fails the rubric, because the deliverable is an audit, not advice.
depth.summary: The audit is the level's synthesis: transcribe the claim, name the assumptions, recompute, price the costs and taxes, verify the people and the documents, locate the promisor of any guarantee, record what remains unknown, and conclude within the evidence. Used habitually, the procedure converts financial marketing from an argument about trust into a set of arithmetic and documentary questions with checkable answers. The level ends where it began, with the position that reading the documents and doing the arithmetic is the skill that survives changes in products, rates, and rules.

visual.title: The eight-move audit on one page
visual.description: A checklist sequence that takes a marketing claim from transcription to a bounded conclusion, with the recomputation and verification steps placed in order.
steps: Transcribe the claim as numbers with units and dates: guaranteed 8%, $50,000, double, nine years.
Recompute: $50,000 at 8% for nine years is $99,950.23, which is 1.999 times, so label the arithmetic as internally consistent rather than as proven.
Price the costs and recheck: 2.25 points of costs leave 5.75% net, giving $82,697.69 in nine years, so the doubling claim fails once the fees are inside the product.

Verify and locate the promisor: check the person through the investment adviser search and BrokerCheck and the product through EDGAR, name who guarantees the 8%, and record the unsupported guarantee and every remaining unknown before stating a bounded conclusion.

questions.prompt: Two retirees hold $500,000 each, withdraw $25,000 at the start of every year, and experience the same set of annual returns over ten years: plus 20% and minus 20% alternating. In the first case the sequence begins with the gain, in the second with the loss. Which retiree ends lower and why?
questions.answer: The retiree whose loss comes first, because the withdrawal removes a larger share of a smaller base
questions.distractor: The retiree whose loss comes last, because the withdrawal is taken before more years of compounding can act on the gain
questions.correction: The arithmetic means are identical at 0% in both cases, so the gap comes from ordering. A fixed dollar withdrawal taken before a fall reduces the capital that would have participated in the recovery, which is why the loss-first path ends lower.

questions.prompt: Which of these exposures is the better candidate for self-insurance with a funded reserve rather than for a purchased policy?
questions.answer: A small, frequent loss whose cost your reserve can absorb without affecting any goal
questions.distractor: A liability judgment that could exceed your savings, because part of it could be repaid out of future income
questions.correction: Insurance earns its cost on losses that are large relative to your resources. Small frequent losses carry the insurer's expense and profit load on every claim and are the easiest to fund from a reserve, while a loss that exceeds your savings is the one that has to be transferred.

questions.prompt: A single premium immediate annuity quotes a 6.0% payout rate at your age, and an advertisement describes that figure as a 6% return. What does the payout rate actually represent?
questions.answer: The annual payment divided by the premium paid, which includes return of principal and mortality pooling
questions.distractor: The interest rate the insurer credits to the contract balance for as long as the payments continue
questions.correction: A payout rate is a ratio of payments to premium, not an interest rate. Part of each payment is your own principal returning, part comes from pooling with other contract holders, and the whole stream depends on the insurer remaining able to pay.

questions.prompt: A parent's will divides everything equally among three children. The retirement account at the same institution carries a beneficiary designation naming only the eldest child and has not been reviewed in eleven years. What happens to the account?
questions.answer: It transfers to the named beneficiary, because the designation moves the asset outside the estate that the will disposes of
questions.distractor: It is divided three ways, because the will is the more complete statement of intent and covers all of the parent's property
questions.correction: A designation is a contract term that transfers the account directly, so the asset never enters the estate for the will to reach. A stale designation is exactly this scenario, which is why the review of forms matters more than the drafting of wishes.

questions.prompt: An advertisement states a 12% average annual return over five years on a strategy and projects $50,000 growing to $88,117.08 at that rate. You recompute the same five annual returns, which are plus 30%, minus 15%, plus 25%, minus 2% and plus 22%, and get $82,571.12. What is the defect in the projection?
questions.answer: The arithmetic average overstates the compound rate, which is 10.55% on those returns
questions.distractor: The projection is arithmetically wrong, because an average of five annual returns can never be used to project a balance
questions.correction: Averaging returns is a legitimate calculation; using the arithmetic average as a compound rate is not. The same returns compounded produce 10.55%, which is the rate a projection must use, and the difference is what the advertisement omitted.

questions.prompt: You are comparing two ways to hold the same fund at the same firm: a brokerage account where you pay a 3.75% sales charge on purchase, and an advisory account where the firm charges 1.00% a year on assets and buys the same fund's no-load share class with an expense ratio 0.20 percentage points lower. Using only the fee table and the firm's Form CRS, list the four figures that must be compared to price each route over your own horizon, and explain why neither route can be declared cheaper without the horizon.
questions.answer: The sales charge, both share classes' expense ratios, the advisory fee, and the year in which cumulative advisory fees overtake the sales charge
questions.distractor: The sales charge, the advisory fee, and the fund's past performance record, since performance determines which structure earns its cost back
questions.correction: Performance describes the fund and is identical in both accounts, so it cannot separate the routes. What separates them is a one-time charge measured once, an ongoing charge measured per year, a small difference in the underlying expense ratio, and the crossover year implied by your holding period.

questions.prompt: An investor wrote a policy statement with a 60/40 target and a five-point band, then during a 30% market fall moved the whole portfolio to cash and rewrote the target as 20/80. Which element of the policy statement failed, and what would the correct arithmetic have required on a $100,000 portfolio that reached $82,000 with $42,000 in stocks?
questions.answer: The pre-committed rebalancing rule failed; the band required buying $7,200 of stocks to restore 60/40
questions.distractor: The risk-tolerance section failed; the correct response was to lower the target allocation and accept the loss without trading
questions.correction: The band is the mechanism that prevents a decision made under the influence of a fall. At $42,000 of stocks out of $82,000 the weight is 51.22%, below the 55% lower edge, so the rule called for moving $7,200 from bonds into stocks to reach $49,200 and $32,800. Changing the target after the fact is the failure the rule existed to prevent.

questions.prompt: A household holds the same two asset types in both a taxable account and a tax-deferred account: a bond fund whose return arrives as interest taxed annually at ordinary rates, and an equity fund whose return arrives mainly as price appreciation. Explain which asset belongs in which account, using the mechanism of annual taxation rather than a rule of thumb, and state the two inputs that can reverse the conclusion.
questions.answer: The bond fund belongs in the tax-advantaged account because its tax is paid every year and cannot compound; the reversal inputs are the withdrawal rate and the preferential rate on long-term gains
questions.distractor: The equity fund belongs in the tax-advantaged account because equities grow more, and deferral is most valuable on the largest balance
questions.correction: The value of sheltering an asset depends on the rate paid annually versus the rate paid on withdrawal, not on the size of the balance. Annual ordinary-income tax compounds against the holder, while appreciation defers, so the interest-producing asset benefits most from shelter unless the withdrawal rate is low enough or the capital gains preference large enough to reverse the ranking.

questions.prompt: A retiree near the withdrawal date holds a target date fund whose glide path stops changing at the target year and an immediate annuity is also being considered. Explain what each instrument does about the risk that the first retirement years produce poor returns, and name the specific exposure each leaves open.
questions.answer: The fund changes the allocation but keeps the market risk; the annuity transfers longevity and payment risk but adds issuer credit risk
questions.distractor: The fund removes the timing risk by becoming conservative, and the annuity removes the inflation risk because payments continue for life
questions.correction: A glide path addresses allocation, and the SEC's own bulletin warns that funds with the same target date can be materially different at that date, so the market exposure remains. A life annuity converts a balance into a payment stream and pools longevity, but the promise depends on the insurer and a fixed payment typically loses purchasing power.

questions.prompt: A variable annuity contract is being considered for money currently in an individual retirement account. Recompute the consequence of the contract's costs on $200,000 over twenty-five years at an assumed 6% gross annual return, comparing total costs of 0.35 percentage points with total costs of 2.25 percentage points, and state the tax conclusion for money already inside an IRA.
questions.answer: About $790,256 against about $502,033, a difference of about $288,222, and the wrapper adds no tax advantage inside an IRA
questions.distractor: About $288,222 against about $790,256, a difference of about $502,033, and the wrapper defers tax that the IRA would otherwise pay annually
questions.correction: The higher-cost contract ends at the lower figure, so the order in the first option is correct and the second option reverses the two balances. The tax conclusion follows the SEC bulletin: money in an IRA is already tax-deferred, so the annuity wrapper contributes only insurance features and their charges.

questions.prompt: A $400,000 tax-deferred account is inherited by an adult child who is not an eligible designated beneficiary, while a $400,000 taxable brokerage account is inherited by the same child. Describe the difference in what the child must do and in the tax character of the money, and state why the answer depends on the beneficiary category.
questions.answer: The retirement account must generally be emptied within ten years, with distributions taxed as ordinary income; the brokerage account receives a basis treatment that differs and has no such deadline
questions.distractor: Both accounts must be emptied within ten years, but only the brokerage account produces taxable income as it is sold
questions.correction: The ten-year rule attaches to the inherited retirement account because of the beneficiary category, and its distributions are income to the beneficiary. The brokerage account has no statutory withdrawal deadline, and its tax character depends on the basis rules in effect at death rather than on a ten-year clock.

questions.prompt: A message claims that a strategy has never had a losing year, has returned an average of 11% annually, and is fully protected. Design the audit steps you would take, naming the three instruments from this level that address the guarantee, the stated average, and the identity of the seller, and state what conclusion the audit permits if the documents cannot be located.
questions.answer: Locate the promisor of the protection, recompute the compound rate from the actual annual returns, and verify the seller's registration; if the documents cannot be located the conclusion is unverified
questions.distractor: Report the claim as false, since an average return of 11% with no losing year is inconsistent with the dispersion of market returns
questions.correction: Inconsistency with typical dispersion is a reason to verify rather than a finding of falsity, and a claim can be arithmetically possible while remaining unverifiable. The audit's permitted conclusions are the three labels, and unverified is distinct from false, which is the standard the capstone lesson sets.

questions.prompt: You are told that a professional is a fiduciary, holds a state insurance license, and earns a commission on the product being recommended. Explain what each of those three facts establishes about the standard that applies and the disclosure you are owed, and name the specific document that would resolve the ambiguity about capacity.
questions.answer: The fiduciary statement and the insurance license describe different regimes, so the resolving document is a Form CRS or its state insurance equivalent
questions.distractor: A fiduciary cannot earn a commission on a recommended product, so the commission proves the fiduciary statement is inaccurate
questions.correction: A fiduciary standard governs process, loyalty and disclosure rather than compensation form, and a person can hold a fiduciary obligation in one capacity and sell under another regime in a different one. Form CRS exists to state the capacity and the conflicts, so it is the document to request rather than an inference to draw.

questions.prompt: A household wants a $600,000 nominal goal in fifteen years and can save $2,000 a month. At an assumed 6% nominal annual return the contributions reach $581,637.42, a shortfall of $18,362.58, and the household's response is to raise the assumed return to 7% instead of raising the contribution. Explain why that response is a defect in the policy statement and what the four honest alternatives are.
questions.answer: The assumption is being used as a control rather than as an input, and the alternatives are to contribute more, extend the horizon, lower the goal, or accept more risk with a wider range of outcomes
questions.distractor: The response is acceptable because a longer horizon supports a higher assumed return, which is the standard approach to closing a shortfall
questions.correction: Changing an assumption does not change the world it describes; it only changes the projection. Raising the assumed return without changing the portfolio's risk changes nothing real, and the four alternatives each change a decision the household actually controls.

questions.prompt: An investor refuses to sell a position that is down 30% because selling would make the loss final, while selling a different position that is up 40% to lock in the gain. Using the tax treatment of realized gains and losses and the lesson on loss aversion, explain the two costs of acting on that preference.
questions.answer: The unrealized loss forgoes its offset against the realized gain, and the decision is being driven by the discomfort of the loss rather than by either position's prospects
questions.distractor: The realized gain is taxed twice because the offsetting loss remains unrealized, and the position that fell will recover because losses reverse
questions.correction: Nothing is taxed twice; the cost is that a real offset goes unused while the $4,000 gain is taxed alone, which at a hypothetical 15% rate is $600 instead of $150 once a $3,000 loss is realized. The second cost is procedural, and the belief that a fall predicts a recovery is the recency error the same lesson warns about.

questions.prompt: A saver plans to leave a retirement account and a payable-on-death bank account to two adult children, and to route everything else through the will. Explain how a beneficiary designation changes both the transfer channel and a dollar amount of protection, giving the federal deposit insurance formula and the cap that applies to an owner with five or more beneficiaries.
questions.answer: The designation transfers both accounts by contract outside the estate, and coverage is owners times distinct beneficiaries times $250,000, capped at $1,250,000 per owner at one bank
questions.distractor: The designation moves the accounts outside the estate, and coverage is a flat $250,000 per depositor regardless of how many beneficiaries are named
questions.correction: The formula multiplies by the number of distinct beneficiaries, so the count matters, while the cap of $1,250,000 per owner applies once five or more beneficiaries are named. The transfer point stands separately: designated accounts bypass the will and, generally, probate.

questions.prompt: You receive a fund fact sheet showing a ten-year annualized return with no statement about fees or taxes. Walk through the four questions the audit requires before that figure can be used in any comparison, and state what the audit may and may not conclude if the prospectus cannot be obtained.
questions.answer: Net or gross of fees, which benchmark, which averaging or weighting method, and over what exact period; if the prospectus cannot be obtained the figure is recorded as unverified
questions.distractor: Whether the return exceeds the inflation rate, whether the manager is registered, whether the fund is a mutual fund or an exchange-traded fund, and over what exact period
questions.correction: The four questions are about the measurement itself rather than about the product's category or the manager, and each changes the number a reader would use. Registration and product type are separate verification steps, and a figure whose basis cannot be documented stays labeled unverified.
